    SAVE THE LAMPASAS’ REPLY BRIEF IN RESPONSE TO SOAH ORDER NO. 35

         Save the Lampasas submits this Reply Brief in Response to State Office of Administrative

 Hearings (SOAH) Order No. 35, which requested that the parties submit responses by October 19,

 2026.1 Accordingly, this Reply Brief is timely filed.

                                                   I.    RESPONSE

         Save the Lampasas submits this reply to the briefs of Oncor Electric Delivery Company

 LLC and LCRA Transmission Services Corporation (collectively, the Applicants) and PUC Staff

 addressing Preliminary Order Issue Nos. 11 and 13.2 In the initial supplemental briefs, Applicants

 divert from their original post-hearing briefing on these two issues, which recognized these two

 issues as being considered under the heading of cost to consumers. 3 The Applicants now attempt

 to leverage Issues Nos. 11 and 13 into an opportunity to provide supplemental briefs on the

Preliminary Order Issues on Need (Issues Nos. 5-7).4 The administrative law judges (ALJs) are

not required to revise the thorough analysis of the record evidence regarding need under

Preliminary Order Issues Nos. 5-7 in the Proposal for Decision (PFD).

        On remand, Applicants’ pivot away from the way in which they briefed these two

Preliminary Order issues in post-hearing briefing does not change the fact that the Applicants have

failed to satisfy their burden of proof on the statutory factor of need (Preliminary Order Issues Nos

5-7. Applicants’ new Brief on Preliminary Order Issues Nos. 11 and 13 cites no evidence other

than what was previously presented to the ALJs in the original post-hearing briefing. The

Applicants’ arguments in their supplemental briefing (some of which PUC Staff support) do not

refute evidence from multiple other parties showing that the Applicants failed to meet their burden

of proof on the issue of need for this line.

        A.       Are the proposed transmission facilities necessary to meet state or federal
                 reliability standards? [Preliminary Order Issue No. 11]

        The ALJs should continue to find under Preliminary Order Issue No. 11 that, while the

Applicants claim this project is a reliability project, they have failed to meet their statutory burden

to establish that the specific Bell County East-to-Big Hill 765-kV line is required to satisfy state

or federal reliability standards.




        4

Nos 11 and 13 “[a]n affirmative answer to Issue No. 11 necessarily informs the need analysis” (Oct. 7, 2026).

                  1.       The Applicants have failed to meet their burden of proof to
                           demonstrate that Bell County East-to-Big Hill 765-kV line is needed to
                           meet state or federal reliability standards.

        As outlined above, on remand, the Applicants attempt to provide supplemental briefing on

the issue of need rather than address the Public Utility Commission of Texas’ (Commission)

specific request.

        Applicants insist there is “no valid reason to reach a different conclusion for Import Path

2” following the Commission’s orders approving Import Paths 1 and 3 in Docket Nos. 59029,

59315, and 59336, that argument ignores the Commission’s statutory duty to independently

evaluate each individual CCN application on its own record. 5 While the order approving the PBRP

authorized the TDUs to file the applications for CCNs, it expressly required that the TDUs would

be required to provide the requisite evidence to carry their burden of proof in each CCN

proceeding:

               10.        For each common local project and import path that requires a
               CCN application, the applicable TSP must establish in the CCN proceeding
               that the certificate meets all applicable legal requirements for a CCN,
               including the requirement set forth in PURA § 37.056(a) that the certificate
               is necessary for the service, accommodation, convenience, or safety of the
               public.6

        The Commission must evaluate the record on its own merits, and, as set forth in the PFD

in response to Preliminary Order Issues No. 5-7, Applicants failed to provide an analysis showing

that this specific proposed project is needed to satisfy any state or federal reliability standard. The

approval of Import Paths 1 and 3 does not automatically authorize the Commission to approve this

application without a record to support its decision. For example, because the record in this docket

fails to show that power is even available at the Bell County East endpoint to transmit westward,

reaching a different conclusion for Import Path 2 is not only valid—it is legally required. 7 It is

valid for the Commission to reach a different conclusion based on the evidence of changed

circumstances that is part of the record in this case, the evidence specific to this project that was

not introduced in the other cases, and the evidence of the unique factors relevant to the grid

conditions surrounding the proposed locations of this project.

                 2.       The Applicants’ record evidence fails to demonstrate that Import
                          Path 2 is required to satisfy state or federal reliability standards.

        The Applicants’ claim that the PBPR, the 2024 RTP, the 2025 RTP, and the April 2026

GTC exit strategy demonstrate that Import Path 2 is required to satisfy NERC Reliability Standard

TPL-001-5.1 and NERC Standard FAC-001-4. These ERCOT reports provide neither a separate

nor a cumulative analysis that supports this assertion.


                          a)       The PBRP does not conduct an analysis of NERC Standards.
                                   Further, the conditions assumed in the 2023 PBRP have
                                   changed, and the PBRP itself asserts only that the projects in
                                   Import Path 2 could be needed in 2038.

        The ERCOT PBRP study evaluated the Bell County East to Big Hill line to address a

projected reliability need in study year 2038. 8 Study year 2038 falls outside NERC’s and

ERCOT’s near-term and long-term planning horizons used in determining compliance with NERC

standard TPL-001-5.1.9           Accordingly, the PBRP recommended that the Commission defer

commitment to 765-kV transmission projects until receipt of information in the 2024 RTP. 10

        The Applicants mischaracterize the PBRP’s purpose and conclusions beyond this point.

The PBRP was required to study ERCOT’s identified regional planning problem and present the

Commission with a portfolio of options to improve system performance and deliver power to

underserved load in the Permian Basin.11 The PBRP explicitly stated that “ERCOT has identified

several import path options for the Commission’s consideration.” 12 According to the language in

the PBRP itself, the Commission must consider the options presented in the planning study and

make a decision supported by the record. 13 Furthermore, a key finding in the PBRP was that 765-

kV lines were preferable to 345-kV lines because of their expanded long-term regional transfer

capability; that general preference does not establish that the Import Path 2 projects were the

exclusive solution.14 In considering the PBRP, the Commission expressly determined that the need

for each project in the PBRP must be shown in the individual CCN applications for each project. 15

The Applicants failed to meet their burden of proof regarding how the changed circumstances

applicable to 45% of the load underlying the PBRP affected the need for Import Path 2. 16 Other

changed circumstances that were brought forward in the evidence yet remain unrefuted by the

Applicants relate to generation being constructed in or near the Permian Basin such that the Bell

55% of the projected load identified in the PBRP.

        ERCOT’s December 12, 2024, sequencing letter indicates that only two of the three 765-

kV import paths are needed by 2030,17 and the Applicants’ own witness conceded, “the words on

the page say that two of the three are needed.” 18 Commission Staff also overstates ERCOT’s

PBRP conclusion by calling the 765-kV backbone the needed solution, while sidestepping a

determination of whether it is necessary to resolve reliability concerns or merely “to support

reliable service.”19 Accordingly, the Commission should wait until more recent, reliable, and

verified estimates are available before committing to a superfluous and presently unsupported 765-

kV transmission project.


                             b)       The 2024 RTP includes the PBRP projects in the base case and
                                      does not provide a separate analysis or study of the impact of
                                      the 765kV import path effects on NERC reliability standards.

supporting the claim that the Bell County East to Big Hill project is required to meet federal

reliability standards. However, the 2024 RTP simply incorporated the PBRP in its initial planning

assumptions.20 The 2024 RTP provides no reasoned analysis demonstrating that Import Path 2

satisfies a specific reliability standard.21

        The 2024 RTP did not show this project would meet a defined 2030 reliability standard. 22

For the RTP, ERCOT evaluates the 6-year regional transmission horizon, testing the grid under

normal operating conditions as well as various single- and multiple-element contingencies, like

the NERC Reliability Standard TPL-001-5.1. 23 The simulated performance is checked against

NERC Reliability Standards and ERCOT Planning Criteria, which cover voltage limits, thermal

line limits, short-circuit levels, and dynamic stability.24 Once a violation is confirmed, ERCOT

formulates a Corrective Action Plan (CAP) to resolve the deficiency. Tellingly, the Project is not

identified as a CAP in the 2024 RTP. The 2024 RTP lists all CAPs in Appendix E. 25 The first

header of that Appendix states that “Projects identified in the Permian Basin Reliability Study with

a 2030 year need are marked with ‘PB’.”26 Neither the current Bell County East to Big Hill 765-

kV project nor Import Path 2 is listed as a needed reliability project in Appendix E, nor are they

described as reliability projects anywhere in the 2024 RTP.27 Appendix F similarly shows 2024

RTP Reliability Project Locations, also without the present project. 28

        Instead, the 2024 RTP states the project was developed “to facilitate the PUC’s discussion

. . . to address statewide reliability needs.”29 Towards that end, the 2024 RTP states that “[t]he

start case for the 765-kV plan incorporated all local projects needed by 2030 in the Permian Basin

application. Applicants’ reliance on NERC Standard FAC-011-4 and the Far West Texas Import

constraints, not that constructing the Bell County East-to-Big Hill line is a mandatory CAP under

NERC standards.40

                   3.     A FERC transmission planning violation is not a violation of state or
                          federal law.

        Chairman Gleeson’s memo inquires “whether failure to comply with the relevant NERC

standards would result in violation of federal law.”41 As discussed above, none of the presented

evidence establishes that Bell County East to Big Hill is necessary to address a transmission

planning need. Even if it did, a transmission planning violation is not a violation of state or federal

law. A FERC transmission planning violation is a technical term fundamentally different from a

federal law violation in its source, nature, and enforcement mechanism. 42 A FERC transmission

planning violation is a forecasted study result showing that certain operating criteria may be

exceeded in the future, based on studies of assumptions about future load, generation, and grid

conditions.43 A planning study showing a risk of a violation of a reliability planning criteria is not

an indicator of lack of compliance with a state or federal rule or law.

        In ERCOT, a planning violation is a technical term of art used during grid modeling and

system assessments.44 It indicates that under a hypothetical future stress scenario (such as peak

summer demand combined with an extreme weather event or equipment failure), the grid’s

existing configuration would fail to meet reliability or performance criteria. 45 Although the PBRP

is not a formal NERC planning study, the record evidence shows that circumstances have changed

relative to the fundamental assumptions underlying that report. Accordingly, even if the PBRP’s

that the report rests on assumptions that have materially changed. 46

       In sum, Save the Lampasas has shown that the existing evidentiary record does not

establish that the proposed Bell County East-Big Hill 765-kV transmission facilities through

Import Path 2 are necessary to meet a state or federal reliability standard.

       B.         What is the estimated congestion cost savings for consumers that may result
                  from the proposed transmission facilities considering both current and future
                  expected congestion levels and the ability of the proposed transmission
                  facilities to reduce those congestion levels? [Preliminary Order Issue No. 13]

       The congestion cost savings referenced in Preliminary Order Issue No. 13 are a very

specific calculation used to support the need for transmission projects not otherwise shown to be

needed for reliability.47 Applicants again pivot from characterizing this test as inapplicable in

post-hearing briefing to pointing to hypothetical congestion savings.

       Applicants did not present a congestion cost savings test in the evidence, and instead,

reference only generalized ERCOT study figures—such as $229 million in annual consumer

energy savings, $890 million in avoided outage costs, and Independent Market Monitor estimates

of $3 billion in West Texas congestion – all of which are metrics that represent system-wide,

cumulative comparisons between entire 765-kV and 345-kV plan concepts. 48 Applicants admit

they conducted no cost-benefit analysis isolated to Import Path 2 or this individual transmission

line to show any congestion-cost savings associated with this project. 49 Historical, grid-wide

congestion figures establish only that congestion exists in Texas; they do not prove that this

specific project will cost-effectively relieve it for consumers. Even if one hypothetically assumed

that the entire PBRP, including Import Path 2, would alleviate all congestion on the system, there

is no evidence that these hypothetical cost savings would be sufficient to support the PBRP as an

“economic project,” given the projected capital costs of the proposed build-out.

        Further, Applicants discuss reduced congestion that would result from the proposed project

if power flows as “exports” from the West to East. 50

        In addition, the Import Path 2 Projects will relieve constraints on the existing 345
        kV network, helping resolve thermal overloads and costly transmission congestion
        that currently burden consumers. The Import Path 2 Projects will also reduce the
        need to curtail exports of cost-effective renewable energy from the Permian Basin,
        further benefiting consumers across the ERCOT system. These benefits will accrue
        across ERCOT, including to consumers outside the Permian Basin.

        Applicants contend that PFD Finding of Fact No. 224 is "flatly incorrect" and assert that

Import Path 2 will operate "bidirectionally" to reduce generation curtailments. 51 However, arguing

that the line will export power eastward directly contradicts the PBRP’s foundational premise—

that West Texas urgently requires imported power. Promoting bidirectional economic flexibility

only highlights Applicants’ failure to prove that this individual facility is necessary to cure a

specific reliability violation. Unquantified secondary benefits cannot substitute for statutory proof

of reliability need.

    As a result, Save the Lampasas agrees with other intervenors that the record contains no

credible evidence that this project’s congestion savings, if any, justify its costs to consumers.

                                       II.   CONCLUSION

       As indicated in Save the Lampasas’s prior briefing on remand, the PFD thoroughly

analyzed the evidence in the record and, as a result, properly answered Preliminary Order Issues

Nos. 11 and 13.

       Based on its Brief and the foregoing Reply Brief, Save the Lampasas reaffirms its

recommendation that the Supplemental PFD could include the following findings:

       (1)    The Application presents this project as one that is proposed to address future

              reliability needs; however, the Applicants failed to meet their burden of proof to

              establish that the proposed project is needed to address federal or state reliability

              standards.

       (2)    The Application addressed this project as a reliability project and asserted no

              justification for the project based on current or future congestion levels or the ability

              of the proposed project to reduce those congestion levels.

       Save the Lampasas respectfully recommends that the PFD make not other changes to its

analysis of Preliminary Order Issues Nos. 5-7 and requests any relief to which it is justly entitled.

                 3.      A FERC transmission planning violation is not a violation of state or
                         federal law.

        Chairman Gleeson' s memo inquires "whether failure to comply with the relevant NERC

standards would result in violation of federal law."41 As discussed above, none of the presented

evidence establishes that Bell County East to Big Hill is necessary to address a transmission

planning need. Even if it did, a transmission planning violation is not a violation of state or federal

law. A FERC transmission planning violation is a technical term fundamentally different from a

federal law violation in its source, nature, and enforcement mechanism.42 A FERC transmission

planning violation is a forecasted study result showing that certain operating criteria may be

exceeded in the future, based on studies of assumptions about future load, generation, and grid

conditions.43 A planning study showing a risk of a violation of a reliability planning criteria is not

an indicator of lack of compliance with a state or federal rule or law.

        In ERCOT, a planning violation is a technical term of art used during grid modeling and

system assessments.44 It indicates that under a hypothetical future stress scenario (such as peak

summer demand combined with an extreme weather event or equipment failure), the grid' s

existing configuration would fail to meet reliability or performance criteria. 45 Although the PBRP

is not a formal NERC planning study, the record evidence shows that circumstances have changed

relative to the fundamental assumptions underlying that report. Accordingly, even if the PBRP's
